title: Which ancient guides should we follow?
source_text: Τίνι δὲ καὶ ἕπεσθαι ἡμᾶς ὁ Κέλσος βούλεται ὡς οὐκ ἀπορήσοντας παλαιῶν ἡγεμόνων καὶ ἱερῶν ἀνδρῶν κατανοητέον. ἀναπέμπει ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ ἐνθέους, ὡς λέγει, ποιητὰς καὶ σοφοὺς (καὶ) φιλοσόφους, μὴ τιθεὶς αὐτοῖς ὀνόματα, καὶ τοὺς ὁδηγοὺς δείξειν ἐπαγγελλόμενος ἀορίστως ἀποφαίνεται τοὺς ἐνθέους ποιητὰς καὶ σοφοὺς καὶ φιλοσόφους. εἰ δ᾿ ἐτίθει τὰ ὀνόματα ἑκάστου τούτων, κἂν ἀγωνίζεσθαι εὔλογον ἡμῖν ἐφαίνετο, ὅτι τυφλώττοντας περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὁδηγοὺς ἡμῖν δίδωσιν, ἵνα σφάλωμεν, ἢ εἰ καὶ μὴ πάνυ τυφλώττοντας, περὶ πολλά γε τῆς ἀληθείας δόγματα ἐσφαλμένους. εἴτ᾿ οὖν Ὀρφέα βούλεται ἔνθεον εἶναι ποιητὴν εἴτε Παρμενίδην εἴτ᾿ Ἐμπεδοκλέα εἴτε καὶ αὐτὸν Ὀμηρον ἢ καὶ Ἡσίοδον, δεικνύτω ὁ βουλόμενος, πῶς βέλτιον ὁδεύσουσιν οἱ τοιούτοις ὁδηγοῖς χρώμενοι καὶ ὠφέληνται περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸν βίον παρὰ τοὺς καταλιπόντας διὰ τὴν Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδασκαλίαν πάντα ἀγάλματα καὶ ἱδρύματα ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσαν Ἰουδαϊκὴν δεισιδαιμονίαν καὶ πρὸς μόνον ἀναβλέποντας διὰ τοῦ λόγου τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν πατέρα τοῦ λόγου θεόν. τίνες δὲ καὶ οἱ σοφοὶ ἢ οἱ φιλόσοφοι, παρ᾿ ὧν βούλεται πολλὰ καὶ θεῖα ἀκοῦσαι ἡμᾶς ὁ Κέλσος, καταλιπόντας θεράποντα θεοῦ Μωϋσέα καὶ προφήτας τοῦ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργοῦ, ἀληθῶς ἐνθέως μυρία ὅσα εἰρηκότας, καὶ αὐτὸν ἐπιλάμψαντα τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ καταγγείλαντα ὁδὸν θεοσεβείας καὶ μηδένα τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ ἄγευστον καταλιπόντα τῶν ἰδίων μυστηρίων, ἀλλὰ δι᾿ ὑπερβάλλουσαν φιλανθρωπίαν ἔχοντα μὲν διδόναι τοῖς συνετωτέροις θεολογίαν, ἐπᾶραι τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπὸ τῶν τῇδε πραγμάτων δυναμένην. οὐδὲν (δ᾿) ἧττον συγκαταβαίνοντα καὶ ταῖς ὑποδεεστέραις ἕξεσιν ἰδιωτῶν ἀνδρῶν καὶ ἁπλουστέρων γυναικῶν οἰκετῶν τε καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς τῶν ὑπὸ μηδενὸς ἢ Ἰησοῦ μόνου βεβοηθημένων πρὸς τὸ, ὡς ἐνεχώρει, βέλτιον αὐτοὺς βιοῦν μετὰ δογμάτων ὧν ἐδύναντο περὶ θεοῦ χωρεῖν;
pass_a_gloss: Whom (τίς) also Celsus wishes us to follow (ἕπομαι), as not going to be at a loss (ἀπορέω) for ancient guides (ἡγεμών) and holy men (ἱερὸς ἀνήρ), must be considered (κατανοητέον). He refers us (ἀναπέμπω) to inspired (ἔνθεος), as he says, poets (ποιητής) and wise men (σοφός) and philosophers (φιλόσοφος), not putting names to them, and promising (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to show the guides (ὁδηγός) he declares indefinitely (ἀορίστως) the inspired poets and wise men and philosophers. If he had put the names of each, it would also have appeared reasonable (εὔλογος) for us to contend (ἀγωνίζομαι) that he gives us guides being blind (τυφλώττω) about the truth, so that we may stumble/err (σφάλλω), or, if not altogether blind, at least mistaken (σφάλλω, pf. pass.) about many doctrines (δόγμα) of truth. Whether then he wishes Orpheus to be an inspired poet or Parmenides or Empedocles or even Homer himself or Hesiod, let the one wishing show how those using such guides will travel (ὁδεύω) better and have been benefited (ὠφελέω) about matters of life (βίος), compared with (παρά) those who, through the teaching of Jesus the Christ, have abandoned (καταλείπω) all statues (ἄγαλμα) and set-up images/shrines (ἵδρυμα), but also all Jewish superstition (δεισιδαιμονία), and look up (ἀναβλέπω) through the Word (λόγος) of God to the only God, the Father of the Word. And who are the wise or the philosophers from whom Celsus wishes us to hear many and divine things, abandoning the servant (θεράπων) of God Moses and prophets of the Maker (δημιουργός) of all, having truly inspiredly (ἐνθέως) said countless things, and him who shone upon (ἐπιλάμπω) the race of men and proclaimed (καταγγέλλω) a way of the worship of God (θεοσέβεια) and left (καταλείπω) no one, so far as in him, untasting (ἄγευστος) of his own mysteries (μυστήριον), but through surpassing love of mankind (φιλανθρωπία) being able to give to the more intelligent (συνετός) theology (θεολογία) able to raise (ἐπαίρω) the soul from the affairs here, [and] no less condescending (συγκαταβαίνω) also to the lower habits/capacities (ἕξις) of unlearned (ἰδιώτης) men and simpler women and household slaves (οἰκέτης), and simply of those helped (βοηθέω) by no one or by Jesus alone, toward living (βιόω) better, as was possible, with doctrines which they were able to contain (χωρέω) about God?
pass_b_english: We must consider whom Celsus wants us to follow, as though we shall not be at a loss for ancient guides and holy men. He sends us back to “inspired poets”, as he calls them, and to “wise men and philosophers”, without giving them names; and though he promises to show us the guides, he speaks in vague terms of “the inspired poets and wise men and philosophers”. If he had given the names of each of them, it would have seemed reasonable for us to contend that he gives us guides who are blind about the truth, so that we should go astray; or, if not wholly blind, at least mistaken about many doctrines of the truth.

Whether, then, he means that Orpheus is an inspired poet, or Parmenides, or Empedocles, or even Homer himself, or Hesiod, let whoever wishes show how those who use such guides travel the road better, and are more helped in the conduct of life, than those who, through the teaching of Jesus Christ, have left behind all statues and images, and indeed all Jewish superstition too, and who, through the Word of God, look up to God alone, the Father of the Word.

And who are the wise men or the philosophers from whom Celsus wants us to hear “many divine things”? Are we to leave behind Moses, the servant of God (Numbers 12:7), and the prophets of the Maker of the universe, who in truth have spoken numberless things by inspiration? And are we to leave him who shone upon the human race and proclaimed the way of the worship of God, and who, as far as lay in him, left no one without a taste of his own mysteries? Rather, through his surpassing love for mankind he is able to give the more intelligent a theology that can lift the soul up from the things of this world; and yet no less does he come down also to the lower capacities of unlearned men and simpler women and slaves, and, in a word, of those whom no one helped but Jesus alone, so that they might live better, as far as they could, with such doctrines about God as they were able to receive.

choices.choice: θεράποντα θεοῦ Μωϋσέα echoes Numbers 12:7 LXX (ὁ θεράπων μου Μωυσῆς), cited at Hebrews 3:5. Koetschau’s supplements (καὶ) before φιλοσόφους and (δ᾿) after οὐδέν accepted. The long final sentence is one question in Greek (τίνες ... χωρεῖν;); split into a question plus explanatory sentences without changing its scope. αὐτὸν ἐπιλάμψαντα refers to Jesus (named at the sentence end); rendered “him who shone upon the human race” without adding the name. ἱδρύματα: objects set up for worship (images, shrines); rendered “images”. ὡς λέγει attaches to ἐνθέους: “inspired poets, as he calls them”. No uncited allusions identified. Review: ἀλλά before δι᾿ ὑπερβάλλουσαν rendered “Rather” (was “For”, which changed the logical link).
'he points only vaguely to' -> 'he speaks in vague terms of' (ἀορίστως ἀποφαίνεται; 'only' not in the Greek)
'For through his surpassing love' -> 'Rather, through' to match ἀλλά
Numbers 12:7 checked (LXX ὁ θεράπων μου Μωυσῆς)
